item.title: Passing the Torch of Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Passing the Torch of Anxiety

How anxious parents raise anxious kids and how to break the cycle.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Anxious parents can unintentionally pass their fears to their children.
  • Breaking the cycle starts with changing how parents respond to their own anxiety.
  • Parents can coach rather than fix.

We give birth to innocent, tiny babies and make an unspoken vow to protect them and keep them happy forever. In those early months, surviving on inconsistent sleep and milk stains, parenting starts to feel manageable once you find your rhythm. You realize you can keep your little one comfortable simply by anticipating their needs, making silly faces, taking spontaneous trips for ice cream, or spending an afternoon at the park.

As our kids grow, life gets a little more complicated, and the emotional stakes rise. If you are an anxious person, that baseline worry doesn't simply disappear when you become a parent. In fact, it peaks and wanes as you navigate each new phase.

Having been an anxious child, teenager, and young adult, I spent years hoping I would somehow spare my own two children from inheriting that "anxiety gene." Yet, as I began observing my daily reactions, my chosen words, my catastrophizing, and even my sudden changes in body language, I reached an eye-opening realization. I was actively passing on anxious information and modeling fear in real-time.

Anxious parenting isn't a character flaw, but rather a protective instinct gone into overdrive. As anxious parents, we hold rigid ideas about ourselves, our children, and what family life "should" look like, clinging to those expectations even when they actively fail us. We become absolute, all-or-nothing thinkers who feel deeply uncomfortable in situations involving uncertainty or perceived danger. Driven by perfectionism and negative assumptions, we often feel more scared than our kids do in unfamiliar settings. Without meaning to, our tense facial expressions, low expectations of our children's resilience, and constant urge to rescue them send a subtle but powerful message: The world is unsafe, and you cannot handle it on your own.

When we panic, we naturally become rigid and controlling to shield our children from potential disappointment or failure. We do things for them so they are done "right," which can end up stifling their independent decision-making, or teaching them to avoid scary situations altogether. Breaking this cycle doesn’t mean you have to eliminate your anxiety overnight or that such a thing is even possible. It does mean that we need to change how we process and respond to that anxiety so that we can stop passing the tension down to our children.

Be Aware

The first step is building self-awareness. Start by tuning in to your physical triggers, such as that sudden tightness in your chest, the clenching of your jaw, or the heart that feels like it’s going to beat out of your chest. Pay close attention to the language you use when speaking to your children, noticing where you might be subtly communicating fear or unsafety about a situation, activity, or task. Phrases like "Be careful!" or "Are you sure you want to try that?" often come from our own nervous systems, not actual danger. Remind yourself that the script you speak aloud today will eventually become your child’s internal monologue tomorrow. By becoming aware of these automatic reactions, you can pause, reframe your words, and consciously choose to build their confidence rather than feed their fear.

Seek Support

Breaking an ingrained cycle of worry isn't something you have to do in isolation, nor should you expect yourself to bear that weight alone. Reaching out for support, whether from a non-anxious partner, a trusted friend, or a licensed therapist, can give you the space to unload and process your triggers before they spill over into your parenting. Talking through an upcoming event or worry with someone outside your immediate spiral helps bring perspective to catastrophic thoughts. If we notice that our anxiety consistently drives our parenting choices, working with a therapist who specializes in adult anxiety can be very helpful. They can equip you with grounding tools so you can process your own fears in adult spaces rather than discharging that nervous energy onto our children.

Coach, Don’t Fix

Be aware that you are likely a fixer, and the ultimate goal is to become a supportive coach to your children rather than frantically trying to fix a situation when something isn’t working out for them. Whether it’s a Lego structure that got knocked over or a tough homework assignment, resist the urge to step in and save the day. Instead of taking over, take a deep breath, speak slowly and in an even, present tone, and ask open-ended questions like: "Ugh, that's tough. What do you think you want to do?” By modeling cognitive flexibility and encouraging brainstorming, you show your child that when problems arise, it’s not a signal for fire alarms to ring, but rather a moment to pause, take note of what happened, and figure out how to handle it calmly.

Parenting as an anxious person is undeniably challenging, and your children’s struggles will inevitably trigger your own anxiety or bring light to your past wounds. But by committing to building your self-awareness, seeking support when you need it, and learning to pause before stepping in, you stop the cycle of anxiety from growing into the next generation. It’s okay for things not to work out perfectly for your child. It’s okay for them to struggle. And it’s completely okay for you to feel uncomfortable through all of it. Take note, take a step back, take a breath, and coach—don't fix. Guide them from a state of calm that your children can then mirror and rely on as their own problem-solving strategy for years to come.

item.title: Your AI Agrees With You Too Much — So Does Your Team
item.description:
Leadership

Your AI Agrees With You Too Much — So Does Your Team

The problem isn't about candor—it's a reward system trained to affirm your beliefs.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • A recent study found that even one AI interaction made users more sure they were right.
  • Just as AI is trained to please users, teams are "trained" to affirm the boss, leaving leaders overconfident.
  • The resulting "Confidence Trap" isn’t a character flaw: It’s a natural consequence of how systems work.
  • The fix: Assign people to dissent, examine what your organization rewards, prompt for disconfirming data.

This post is co-authored by Emily Irving and Jeff Wetzler.

Imagine you're wrestling with a difficult organizational decision and decide to stress-test your thinking with an AI assistant. You explain your reasoning, share the plan, ask for feedback. The AI engages thoughtfully by refining a detail here, affirming your logic there, and it praises you for thinking through the situation so carefully. You close the laptop feeling sharper and more confident than when you opened it.

Most sophisticated AI users would recognize the trap immediately. This is called sycophancy: a model's tendency to tell users what they want to hear rather than what is accurate. A recent Stanford study revealed something even more unsettling than the sycophancy itself: what it does to the people on the receiving end. After just one interaction with an LLM, users became measurably more convinced they were right, less willing to examine their own role in a problem, and more likely to trust and return to the system that had affirmed them — even when it was distorting their judgment.

Source: Walls.io / Pexels

Now imagine a leader presenting a new strategy to her team. She walks through the plan, explains her reasoning, and invites reactions. One team member says the direction "makes sense" and asks a clarifying question about implementation. Another calls it "a strong foundation" and suggests a minor refinement. What neither says, though both are thinking it, is that they have serious reservations about whether the plan will actually work. They've read the room, sensed the leader's investment in the idea, and made a quiet calculation about what's (not) worth raising.

The underlying dynamic is identical. In both cases, the person making the decision leaves more confident – not because their idea was genuinely challenged, but because the system around them has been trained over time to affirm what they already believe. We call this the Confidence Trap, and it is far more common, and far more costly, than most leaders recognize.

It's not about incompetence or bad intent

The Confidence Trap isn't a personality problem or a failure of candor. Research shows it's structurally built into most organizations. One widely cited study found that 85% of employees had at some point withheld an important concern from their boss. And power dynamics distort leaders’ perceptions due to forces from both sides: People with less power become more cautious about what they say upward, while people with more power become less attuned to others’ true beliefs and thinking.

What makes this trap so hard to catch is that leaders’ false confidence feels earned. When a leader's perspective is repeatedly reinforced, it can feel as though an idea has been rigorously stress-tested when, in reality, meaningful challenge has softly disappeared. Leaders grow ever more certain while losing contact with the information that would help them see more clearly. And the faster the environment moves (the more decisions get made, the more tech tools promise to speed things up) the less time there is for the slow, friction-laden conversations where candor actually surfaces.

The good news is that the AI research community has been forced to address the sycophancy problem, and what they've learned translates directly to leadership:

Institutionalize the red team

AI labs don't just ask their models to "be more honest." They assign red teams whose formal job is to break things, surface failure modes, and expose where the system is telling users what they want to hear rather than what is true. This is a structured, resourced, institutionalized role — not a suggestion, but a mandate.

Most organizations have no equivalent, but leaders can create one: Designate someone — a chief of staff, a trusted board member, a rotating senior role — whose explicit responsibility is to surface the strongest case against the prevailing view before major decisions are made. This isn't about devil's advocacy as a meeting tactic. It's about making challenge a defined accountability rather than an act of interpersonal courage.

The difference between "does anyone have concerns?" and "Marcus, I'd like you to spend 24 hours building the strongest possible case against this direction and bring it back to the group" is the difference between theater and genuine stress-testing.

Audit your reward signals

One of the most important insights from AI development is that sycophancy isn't a random bug — it's what the system learned to do because agreement got rewarded. A widely used training technique called Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback inadvertently bakes in agreeableness because humans tend to rate confident, validating responses more highly than challenging ones. Nobody intended it, but the incentive structure produced it anyway.

Organizations work exactly the same way. Ask yourself honestly: what do our promotion decisions, meeting dynamics, and performance signals actually reward? If the people who rose fastest were those who aligned most visibly with leadership priorities, your organization has trained itself to be sycophantic (regardless of what your core values say). Fixing this requires auditing the reward signal, not just calling for more candor.

When leaders publicly recognize someone for delivering uncomfortable news, or for changing the direction of a decision, they recalibrate the system. When they react defensively to challenge, they reinforce it, often silencing candor across dozens of future interactions. People are watching how you respond in the moments that matter far more closely than they're listening to what you say you want.

Prompt for disconfirming information

Sophisticated AI users have discovered that broad prompts produce agreeable responses, while specific adversarial prompts produce more honest ones. Ask a model "what do you think of this plan?" and you're practically asking to be flattered. Ask "what is the single most likely reason this fails?" and you get something considerably more useful.

Leaders can apply exactly the same logic to how they gather input from people. The question design determines the quality of the information that comes back. "Any feedback?" subtly frames consensus as the expected outcome. More specific prompts change the assignment entirely:

  • "What's the strongest case against this?"
  • "What is most likely to get in the way of this being successful?"
  • "Where are you already seeing this get stuck in practice?"

Questions like these make surfacing challenge part of the job rather than an act of courage. They also signal something important: that you're genuinely more interested in accuracy than in agreement. People notice that difference, and over time, it changes what they're willing to bring to you.

AI labs have spent years learning that you can't fix a sycophantic system by asking it nicely to be more honest. The bias is structural, baked into the underlying incentives, and the fix has to be structural too. Organizations work exactly the same way. The leaders who escape the Confidence Trap aren't the ones who ask for candor the loudest. They're the ones who make candor structurally inevitable by designing their environments so that the honest answer is also the easy one to give.

So the next time you walk out of a meeting feeling confident that your plan has been tested, pause. Ask yourself: Was it actually challenged? Or did the system just do what systems do — and tell you what you wanted to hear?

_______

Emily Irving is the CEO of Ask and co-creator of the Ask Approach.

Jeff Wetzler is the author of Ask: Tap Into the Hidden Wisdom of People Around You, and co-founder of Transcend.

item.title: What "The Odyssey" Taught Me About My Phone
item.description:
Social Media

What "The Odyssey" Taught Me About My Phone

The answer isn't less technology. It's deciding in advance how you'll use it.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Tech insiders limit their children’s technology use, and countries are now banning social media for minors.
  • But abstinence is neither practical nor wise: opting out means opting out of real power.
  • The answer is intentional use, built not on willpower but on choice architecture.
Source: photoguns / Adobe Stock

No man can resist the song of the sirens. Their music is so enchanting that every sailor who hears it steers toward the rocks and is destroyed.

Odysseus knew this. So when his ship approached their island, he didn’t try to resist. He had his crew plug their ears with beeswax — and he had himself chained to the mast.

I was reminded of this watching the new film The Odyssey the other day, and it struck me that in those chains lies the key to our freedom in the world of modern tech.

The Chefs Who Don’t Eat the Food They Cook

The first thing to accept is that there is something dangerous about tech. One piece of evidence is both simple and alarming: the people who know technology best are famously the most cautious about using it, particularly where their children are concerned. As early as 2010, Steve Jobs famously told a reporter that his kids hadn’t used the newly released iPad: “We limit how much technology our kids use at home.” In 2025, former Facebook executive Sarah Wynn-Williams testified before the U.S. Senate that Meta executives had told her their own teenagers weren’t allowed on Facebook or Instagram.

This instinct is now being reflected at the social level. Australia became the first country to ban social media for children under 16 in December 2025, and Denmark, France, Malaysia, and the U.K. are following with bans of their own.

Behind these moves sits a growing body of evidence: the U.S. Surgeon General warned that social media carries a “profound risk of harm” to adolescent mental health, and research keeps accumulating — on fractured attention, on sleep, and on the “cognitive debt“ we take on when we outsource our thinking to machines.

The conclusion seems obvious: Unplug. Get out while you can.

But that won’t work, and it’s not the right answer anyway.

Why Abstinence Fails

The first reason is practical: opting out is close to impossible. Try doing your banking today without a smartphone. Try parking your car, boarding a flight, or receiving your child’s school announcements. Modern life functions on the assumption that you are plugged in, and the person who is not achieves frustration rather than serenity.

The second reason is that these technologies are not merely traps. They are also powers. In my pocket I carry most of humanity’s accumulated knowledge, the ability to reach anyone on Earth, and tools of creation that a studio couldn’t have assembled 30 years ago. Renouncing all that makes you less capable of learning, building, connecting, and contributing. Refusing these powers does not seem like wisdom to me.

So we can’t leave, and we shouldn’t even want to. Once we see this, we can ask the subtler, more important question underneath, the question that I spent an entire book answering in the context of AI: How do we make sure that we are using these powers rather than being used by them?

Using the Tool vs. Being Used By It

Here are two archetypal modes of using tech. In Mode 1, we choose to pick up the device for a particular purpose — someone to email, a route to find. In Mode 2, we pick it up without thinking, just fiddling with it while waiting for a bus, scrolling videos to push away difficult feelings or even just because boredom is hard to bear.

Like everyone else, I know that second mode intimately. I’ve caught myself standing in my own kitchen, coffee going cold, scrolling through something I never chose to read. Nobody made me do it. But I didn’t exactly decide to, either. In this mode, the deciding has been done for us — by an algorithm whose goals are not our goals.

Researchers have a name for Mode 1 done well: “digital balance." Digital balance has three parts: knowing what you came to do, keeping an eye on how long you’re staying, and checking that the use actually serves what you value. People who used tech with digital balance — Mode 1 — showed markedly better attentional control and psychological well-being than the people who mostly used it in Mode 2.

Conceptually, that’s the fix — use the tech to serve your goals, rather than letting it use you to fulfill the goals of its owners. More Mode 1, less Mode 2.

But knowing the fix and living the fix are two very different things. And this is particularly true in modern tech, because it has been engineered by very smart people with the explicit aim of pulling us into Mode 2.

So how do we turn insight into action?

Don’t Resist the Machine. Rearrange It

Odysseus gave us the answer, and it is confirmed by modern psychology. Angela Duckworth, James Gross, and colleagues have shown that the most effective self-control doesn’t happen in the moment of temptation at all — it happens upstream in how we design our situations. In field experiments, students who changed their environments beat those who tried to white-knuckle it.

This is called choice architecture, and it’s simply Odysseus’s mast in scientific language. The lesson is simple: Instead of using willpower to fight the sirens in the moment, create situations that make Mode 2 difficult or even impossible to reach.

Here is how you can start doing that immediately.

4 Things You Can Try Today

  1. Make things pull, not push. Be intentional about your notifications. When in doubt, turn them off.
  2. Batch the checking. Give email and messages specific windows, and close the windows when you’re done.
  3. Demote the phone. Move sustained work to a laptop. Let the phone go back to being a tool rather than a portal.
  4. Fence off one sacred zone. Meals, the bedroom, the first half-hour after waking — one space where devices simply do not solicit you.

The Cunning Odysseus

Odysseus defeated the sirens before he engaged with them: on the deck of the ship, in advance, with rope. So when the song began, there was no choice left to make. That is the model.

The insiders and the legislators are right about the danger, and the way to deal with it is to decide, before the music starts, what kind of sailor you’re going to be.
